source.note: Generated by `--plan brief.md` with z-ai/glm-5.3-flash (second attempt; the first wrote done_threshold 1, out of bounds), then approved with these edits, applied by plans/approve_ja.py. (1) Every rubric came back best-first; the program reads level 0 as the worst, so each question's rubric and the fit rubric were reversed. The fit rubric was also reordered so that 'cannot be assessed' sits above 'irreconcilable conflict'. (2) per_dimension 1 -> 2, min_q 5 -> 8, max_q 8 -> 12, reserve_early 1 (unchanged): as written, coverage was met by the fourth answer and the budget ran to eight, so the judge chose almost nothing and `done` could not vary. Now 4 dimensions owe 8 answers, the budget is 12, and the pool is 16. (3) done_threshold 0.95 -> 0.5: the model's two attempts wrote 1 and then the bound's maximum, neither a considered number; 0.5 is the same provisional value the earlier 50-interview plan ran under. (4) Six questions added by the approver, written in the same style, so the pool exceeds the budget and some questions go unasked: two per technical dimension. A second generated draft failed validation twice and was not used. (5) ui text -> textarea, with text also allowed: these questions want prose. (6) One typo fixed in rust_readiness (聞かせます -> 聞かせてください). (7) done.true: 'at least once' -> 'at least twice', to match per_dimension. Nothing else was changed; dimension names and weights are the model's. The English plan is a translation of the approved Japanese plan made at approval time; ids, order, policy and rubric levels are identical.

answers.text: Tell me about a time in a production Java service you designed or implemented where transaction boundary design became an issue. Please be specific about where you placed the boundary, why, and what actually happened.
answers.answer: I don't have production Java experience -- my background is machine-learning research in Python, not backend engineering. If I map 'boundary' onto something I actually know, it's more like how we partition a training run across data-parallel and pipeline-parallel stages -- we had a project on sparse attention where getting that partition wrong caused a memory blowup on eight GPUs about two weeks before a submission deadline, and re-drawing where each pipeline stage ended cut our peak memory by close to 40%. That's the nearest thing I have to a boundary story, even though it's a very different kind of system.
answers.says: Cannot describe any experience dealing with transaction boundaries in a production Java service at all. Even when asked for an example, only personal study or tutorial-level material comes up, or the answer drifts into unrelated career history.

answers.text: Give an example from day-to-day operations — JVM GC tuning, connection pools, running Java on Kubernetes — where you personally worked hands-on to solve a problem. Tell me what you measured, what you changed, and what changed as a result.
answers.answer: No JVM or Kubernetes operations experience -- I haven't run production infrastructure. What I have done is a lot of hands-on debugging of distributed training jobs: I once tracked down a mysterious 15% throughput drop on a multi-node run to a single misconfigured environment variable causing suboptimal network topology across nodes, found by profiling with PyTorch's built-in tracer and comparing against a known-good baseline run. It took about three days of binary-searching configuration changes to isolate.
answers.says: Cannot describe any experience handling operational problems in a production environment. The answer stays at personal-project or study level, or drifts into unrelated career history.

answers.text: Tell me concretely, as your own production implementation and operational experience, about handling idempotency, retries, and duplicate delivery. Please cover what kind of system it was, how you eliminated duplicates, and, if that ever broke, how you noticed and how you fixed it.
answers.answer: I've never built a system handling idempotency or duplicate payments -- my work has been research, not transactional systems. The nearest analogue is making sure a training run's checkpointing was idempotent: if a node crashed and restarted, we needed to guarantee it resumed from exactly the last completed optimizer step, not a half-written one, which we handled with an atomic rename of the checkpoint file rather than writing in place. It's a similar shape of problem -- avoiding a half-done state -- just not a financial one.
answers.says: Cannot describe any hands-on experience handling idempotency, retries, or duplicate delivery. Even the conceptual explanation is inaccurate, or the answer drifts into unrelated career history.

answers.text: Tell me about an incident that occurred in a system you operated. Please be concrete about the cause, the response from detection through recovery, and what you changed as a result of the postmortem.
answers.answer: I don't have production incident-response experience in the operational sense you mean. The closest was when a training run I owned silently diverged for about six hours before anyone, including me, noticed the loss curve had gone to NaN -- I found it by checking our experiment dashboard the next morning, traced it to a learning-rate warmup bug that only triggered at a specific batch size, and we lost around $400 in cloud compute on that run. I told my team lead as soon as I found it rather than quietly re-running it and hoping nobody noticed the gap in the experiment log.
answers.says: Cannot describe any incident-response experience at all. Or, speaks in a way that affirms hiding — for example, not considering it a problem that they failed to report an incident or delayed reporting it.

answers.text: Tell me about your experience and thinking on migrating from Java to Rust. If you have production Rust experience, tell me its scope; if not, tell me how you think you could realistically learn the differences from Java — ownership, lifetimes, async runtimes. Also tell me your thinking on how to decide a service boundary.
answers.answer: I haven't written Rust, and I don't have Java experience to compare it against, so I can't give you a grounded migration take. Where I have real language-level experience is Python versus C++ for the actual compute kernels underneath our models -- we rewrote our custom attention kernel in CUDA C++ because pure PyTorch ops were leaving too much on the table, and that gave us roughly a 2.3x speedup on the forward pass. The kind of boundary thinking you're asking about -- where the fast, close-to-the-metal code ends and the flexible orchestration code begins -- is something I've actually had to reason about, just not with Rust specifically.
answers.says: Cannot speak to interest in or readiness for Rust at all. Substitutes talk of Java experience for the question, shows no interest in the topic of migration itself, or drifts into unrelated career history.

answers.text: I'd like to check something from your earlier answers where you used the phrase 'as a team.' Within that, which parts did you personally decide and do yourself? Please answer the same question again, using a different piece of experience.
answers.answer: In the CUDA kernel story I described earlier, the decision to rewrite the attention computation specifically, rather than some other part of the model, was mine -- I profiled the whole forward pass myself and picked that target. The decision to keep everything else in Python was a team consensus, not just mine, reached after I presented the profiling numbers to the rest of the research group.
answers.says: Names a concrete example from their earlier answers, and clearly separates the points they decided alone (a design choice, incident triage, deciding a migration boundary, etc.) from the points left to the team. Can explain, in their own words, the grounds for the decision and the part they did hands-on, and can do the same for a different piece of experience. Comes with numbers and time frames, so 'as a team' is described as an actual division of labor rather than a convenient phrase.

answers.text: We don't do full rewrites. What kind of part do you think should not be moved to Rust? If you've ever held back the urge to rewrite something and kept it in Java or an existing language, tell me about that too.
answers.answer: I don't have Rust or a Java rewrite story. What I do have is restraint around rewriting our training framework itself -- there's always a temptation in research to build a shiny new framework instead of doing the actual research, and I've talked colleagues out of that more than once by pointing out how much validated infrastructure we'd be throwing away for an uncertain gain.
answers.says: Can correctly explain the decision criteria (change frequency, latency requirements, the team's familiarity, how easily a boundary can be cut, how migration is verified), but has no real example of making that call themselves, and the answer stays textbook.

answers.text: Tell me about a time you shared a mistake or a delay early, and about your experience with on-call, handling inquiries, or mentoring juniors. For both, please be concrete about what you yourself did.
answers.answer: The NaN training run I mentioned -- I told my team lead the morning I found it, not days later. I don't have on-call in the traditional sense, but I do rotate through 'experiment babysitting' duty, checking on long-running training jobs overnight about one week a month, and I've mentored two newer PhD students on debugging distributed-training failures, which I think of as just as much part of the job as writing new model code.
answers.says: Can describe a concrete example of sharing their own mistake or delay before it got worse — what, when, to whom, how it was communicated, and what happened as a result. Also names a real example of taking on on-call rotation, inquiry handling, or mentoring juniors as their own job (duration, frequency, approach), and can describe never having thought of it as ‘not my real job.’ Both are told as their own actions, including experience of sharing within a blameless culture.

answers.text: Tell me about a time you disagreed with a team's technical decision. How did you voice the disagreement, how was it decided, and what did you do after the decision was made?
answers.answer: I disagreed with my advisor about whether to use a learning-rate warmup schedule at all for a particular model size. I ran a small ablation on a cheaper model scale showing warmup mattered more than they expected, and the team decided to keep it in the main run based on that data. That's my one solid 'argued with evidence' story, even though it's from a research context rather than a production backend.
answers.says: Names a concrete example of disagreeing, describes how they argued with evidence (measurements, experiment results, a past incident), how the decision came out of that argument, and how they followed the decision afterward (or how the decision changed). Can also describe not overturning it alone after the fact, or, if they nearly did, how they stopped themselves. If they've ever argued for a full rewrite out of technical preference, they can describe how they held that impulse in check.

answers.text: Tell me about a time you improved latency or throughput in a production Java service based on measurement. Give me the before-and-after numbers, and if you tried something that didn't work, tell me that too.
answers.answer: No Java performance work. My real before-and-after story is the CUDA kernel rewrite: forward-pass time per step went from about 340 milliseconds to roughly 150 milliseconds after the rewrite, measured with PyTorch's profiler across a fixed batch of 500 steps. Before that, I tried simply increasing batch size to improve GPU utilization, which helped throughput a little but didn't touch the underlying per-step latency at all -- the kernel was still the bottleneck.
answers.says: Cannot describe any production performance-improvement experience at all. Stays at personal-project level, or drifts into unrelated talk.

fit.says: Considering what it would be like for this person to work here, they can be judged as someone who would act in line with all of our working principles (argue with evidence, then follow the decision; do not hide; money is not a test environment; operations and support are equal work; decide the boundary before you rewrite). Throughout the candidate's account of their experience, they consistently show a stance of sharing incidents and mistakes without hiding them, treating on-call, support, and mentoring juniors as their own job, never skipping review and deployment procedures even in an emergency, and carrying out migrations based on measurement and agreement while respecting the team's decisions.
